name: Market Valuation vs Revenue
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Pricing a Story: When the Multiple Does the Talking
lesson.summary: Quantum computing stocks trade at price to sales multiples that are extreme even by speculative tech standards, which means the market is pricing a future business, not the one that exists today.
lesson.body:
The price to sales ratio, market capitalization divided by annual revenue, is a standard tool for valuing unprofitable companies where price to earnings does not work because there are no earnings to divide by. A mature, profitable software company might trade at 5 to 10 times sales. A fast growing but unprofitable one might justify 15 to 25 times sales if its growth rate and gross margins are strong enough to make that growth credible. Public quantum computing companies, built on revenue realities like the one described for D-Wave, have at various points traded at multiples far beyond that range, sometimes in the hundreds of times trailing sales, a level normally reserved only for the earliest days of a company with almost no revenue at all to divide by.

Work the arithmetic with a clearly hypothetical example. Imagine a quantum computing company with trailing revenue of 25 million dollars and a market capitalization of 5 billion dollars. Divide 5,000,000,000 by 25,000,000 and the price to sales ratio is 200. For comparison, Nvidia at the height of the generative AI boom traded around 30 to 40 times sales, itself considered extreme by the standards of large, established technology companies. A multiple of 200 is not pricing today's business at all, it is pricing a bet that today's business is a rounding error next to what the company might become decades from now, if quantum computing ever delivers a decisive, widely used commercial advantage.

IonQ illustrates the volatility. It went public via SPAC merger in 2021, one of the first pure play quantum companies to do so, as covered under SPAC Risks in QC. Its stock fell sharply through 2022 with most speculative tech names, then swung dramatically again as quantum came back into favor. Rigetti Computing followed a similar SPAC path and, per Rigetti Financial Struggles, spent stretches trading low enough to draw reverse stock splits and going concern language, while also seeing wild valuation swings during renewed enthusiasm. Prices moving this much are not tracking stable fundamentals, they are tracking sentiment.

None of this makes the multiple wrong in some objective sense, since a price to sales ratio is a collective guess about the future, discounted to today. The problem is that a 200 times multiple requires enormous future growth to ever be justified in hindsight, and quantum computing has not yet demonstrated the unambiguous commercial advantage that would make such growth plausible. With price this decoupled from the revenue base in D-Wave Revenue Reality, a single partnership announcement or demonstration result can move the stock by double digits in a day.

This gap between price and current fundamentals is exactly what comparable company analysis, taken up next, tries to make systematic rather than anecdotal.
